Your questions about the housing crisis answered

What is the right to housing? What would change if housing was recognised as a human right in Australian law? In this episode of Curiosities, we speak with Professor Jessie Hohmann about Australia's housing crisis, why safe and secure housing matters, who is being left behind, the challenges of renting and home ownership, and what a fairer housing system could look like. 

Hello curious people. I'm Professor Jessie Hohmann, a human rights lawyer at UTS.

This is Law Curious.

[Intro music}

Let's get started.

Will building more homes actually make housing more affordable?

This is one of the great myths in the Australian housing debate. In the last census, there were a million empty homes in Australia. This far exceeds the serious numbers of people on waitlists for housing, experiencing housing insecurity or housing unaffordability.

Even though those numbers are very high, the problem in Australia is not that we don't have enough housing.

The problem is how housing is distributed amongst the population. Because housing is increasingly treated as an investment vehicle, it becomes more and more expensive and out of reach to more and more people.

So the idea that we need more homes to solve the housing crisis, or to ensure that people enjoy the right to adequate housing, while important, particularly in increasing our supply of housing outside of market options, for example, social housing or community land trusts, for example, is not the only solution, and it shouldn't be the primary one.

We need to think much more seriously in Australia about how to distribute housing that already exists and how to make that housing affordable, and that will make a greater difference than the supply of new housing in the short term.

What is the right to housing?

The right to housing is included in the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, which Australia signed up to in the 1970s.

Australia was in fact one of the countries that pushed hard for the inclusion of a right to an adequate standard of living, and the right to adequate housing is a component of that.

At its heart, the right is a place to live in peace, dignity and security.

This has been interpreted to include, amongst other elements, security of tenure, affordability, access to adequate materials, services, facilities and infrastructure, location and cultural adequacy.

The right is a really important part of our social fabric.

It's at the heart of our society.

Everyone needs a place where they can be
safe, secure and free.

If housing is a human right, how can the law be used to protect it?

This is something that should frustrate everyone.

When Australia signed up to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, it took on international obligations for the right to housing.

However, it decided not to make the right available before any Australian court or tribunal.

In my view, the government is cheating Australians.

It's empowering itself through international law but refusing to allow Australians to hold it to account.

Why do people with good jobs still struggle to buy a home or pay the rent?

This is a really important question, and it's one that we can't understand without understanding the broader context of social rights enjoyment in Australia.

We tend to think of Australia as a countrywhere people enjoy a great standard of living, but we've really never treated housing as a right.

And in fact, housing is and has generally been a commodity in the Australian context.

The result of this is that housing increasingly becomes divorced from a place for people to live. Instead, it becomes a speculative investment vehicle traded across global markets.

With this, it becomes increasingly expensive, and a smaller and smaller slice of the population is able to access housing.

If governments know there's a housing crisis, why does it feel like nothing changes?

For a long time it's been politically possible for governments to ignore the housing crisis. John Howard famously said while he was Prime Minister that he'd never had a voter complain about the cost of their house increasing.

In a society where many people are in their own homes, there hasn't been sufficient political pressure for change.

But now the depth and breadth of the housing crisis is pushing us in new directions, and politicians are needing to respond.

So far, the proposed solutions have focused on supply and have leaned heavily on market-based solutions.

But supply is not our primary problem.

Our primary problem is the distribution of housing.

And as more and more people are unable to access home ownership due to the expense and the concentration of housing in the hands of investors, it's only now, with the scale and breadth of the housing crisis, that there's sufficient pressure for change.

What are we getting wrong when it comes to solving the housing crisis?

From my perspective as a human rights lawyer, the first way to answer this question is to ask, what does a right to housing as a human
right provide for us?

How can it answer our housing needs?

If we put the question of does this housing policy, does this housing law give us steps towards a place to live in peace, dignity and security?

It can help to reframe all of our policy debates.

And yet we so seldom ask that question in Australia.

We also need to move beyond homeownership as our dream and our goal.

Homeownership can provide a place to live in peace, security and dignity. But so can rental housing. So can housing that is taken out of the market, social housing or public housing, or other non-market options like co-operative housing.

By only seeing our housing dreams through the filter of ownership, we block out so many other options which can provide creative solutions
to our housing problems.

Do other countries do housing differently to Australia and what can we learn from them?

It's a great idea to look beyond our national borders, to think about how to solve a housing crisis and how to improve our housing systems.

Countries in Europe provide some great contrast to Australia. In some countries, leases can be as long as 99 years – a significant increase in security of tenure.

Thinking differently about our rental tenancies legislation and the balance of power between landlords and tenants.

It's also possible for us to think about taking significantly more of our housing stock outside the market. Some countries have historically had very high levels of social housing. Austria, and particularly Vienna, is famous for the levels of social housing. More than a third of people in Vienna live in social housing. The housing is a very good quality and it attracts no social stigma. Imagine if we could create options like that in Australia.

Another option is thinking about property differently. In some South American constitutions, property isn't a right, it's a social function. And that means that you need to use your property for society's benefit. That's a whole new way of thinking about property and the balance between the state society and the individual.

And again, that's a point we can take for inspiration.

One way to achieve all these aims is to put housing as a right at the centre of all of our policy debates. 

Which groups in Australia face the greatest barriers to safe, secure
and affordable housing, and why?

When the Australian delegate suggested including a right to adequate housing in international law, I think they thought this right was already ensured in Australia.

Standards of living were generally high after the Second World War, and there was great faith in progress, but it was a thin vision even then.

Migrants, Australia's Indigenous peoples and those living in poverty always struggled to access adequate and secure housing.

Fast forward to today and this situation remains.

But the categories have expanded to include young people, older women and women and children fleeing domestic and family violence.

So what's at the root of this? Why, in a prosperous, democratic country, haven't we been able to solve our housing crisis?

We haven't put the right housing at the heart of our housing policy, or asked it to answer our housing questions.

Instead, we've expected the market to do all the work for us and in doing so, we've given politicians a free ride.

If housing was recognised as a human right in Australia, what would change?

We may be about to find out. The Australian Capital Territory has just
reformed its human rights charter, and the right to housing will become part of Australian Capital Territory law.

This is a really exciting development, but I do approach it with a note of caution. In other jurisdictions in Australia that have human rights charters, such as Victoria or Queensland, human rights have been interpreted thinly and conservatively.

A lot will depend on the daring arguments that can be brought before the court by human rights advocates and activists, and it will depend on the judiciary expanding their frames of reference and thinking seriously about the international human rights obligations that Australia bears, but which it hasn't made available to its citizens.

What makes you the most frustrated about the current housing situation?

What frustrates me most is the narrowness of our vision.

When we look at the housing crisis, we tend to assume that homeownership will solve all our problems. We tend to look to market solutions and we tend to focus on supply.

Thinking seriously about the right to housing gives us a way to broaden our horizons. It gives us an opportunity to look internationally, and it gives us a way to reframe our debates with the human being and their need for safe, secure and adequate housing at the centre.

That was all the questions for today.

I hope you learned something new.

Until next time, stay curious.

Why UTS?

Study in the heart of Sydney’s technology precinct at Australia’s #1 ranked young university. Our courses are highly-regarded, developed in partnership with industry leaders using practice-based learning approaches. No matter what path you choose, you'll learn the skills to become an innovative and creative thinker, driving positive change in society.
